title: Wasserturm Prenzlauer Berg - FAQ
subtitle: The tower, the reservoirs, 1933 and how to visit the hill.

items.q: Where exactly is the Wasserturm in Prenzlauer Berg?
items.a: On the hill park **Wasserturmplatz** between **Knaackstraße**, **Belforter Straße**, **Diedenhofer Straße** and **Kolmarer Straße** in the Kollwitzkiez. The nearest U-Bahn is **U Senefelderplatz** on the U2, and the **M2** tram stops at Prenzlauer Allee/Metzer Straße.

The waterworks on the hill opened on **1 January 1856**, run by the English **Berlin Waterworks Company**. The big round tower you see today was built from **1875 to 1877**, designed by **Henry Gill**.

items.q: Can you go inside the Wasserturm?
items.a: No. The floors under the old tank were built as flats and are still private homes; the Bezirksamt Pankow says **ten flats** are lived in. You can walk all around it in the park.

items.q: Can you visit the underground reservoirs?
items.a: Only during exhibitions or events. Since **1994** the association **Förderband e.V.** has organised art and sound projects there for the district, and the small reservoir at **Diedenhofer Straße 20** is used for exhibitions. I found **no regular opening hours**, so check the listings first.

items.q: What happened at the Wasserturm in 1933?
items.a: In spring 1933 the **SA** used the cellars of the first machine house as an early **concentration camp** for political opponents, until about **mid-June 1933**. The building was blown up in **1935** and the park opened in **1937**. No full records survive, so the number of prisoners is not known.

A red brick memorial wall from **1981** with a plaque stands at the corner of **Knaackstraße and Kolmarer Straße**. A glass panel added in 2005 was smashed in **February 2024**; when I checked on **27 November 2026** I found no sign it had been replaced.

items.q: Is it the oldest water tower in Berlin?
items.a: It is often called that, but the careful wording is **the oldest surviving tower of Berlin's public water supply**. A small private water tower of the 1830s still stands in the park of **Glienicke Palace**.

items.q: Why is it called Dicker Hermann?
items.a: It is a Berlin nickname, **fat Hermann**, for the tower's wide, round shape. The tower was also on the **Prenzlauer Berg coat of arms** from 1920 to 1992.

items.q: Is the park accessible with a buggy or wheelchair?
items.a: The hill is steep and the main way up is by **steps**, including two stair accesses on the south slope. I could not confirm a step-free route, so plan for stairs.
